title: Science and Technology: Unit-wise Subjective Question Bank
html:
Groups B and C carry 40 of the 50 written marks, and they are won by writing, not by recognising. A two-mark question wants two scoring points; a four-mark question wants four.

This chapter gives, unit by unit, the short and long questions the pattern keeps producing, each followed by answer notes — the scoring points in order, the way an examiner reads them.

Write your own answer on paper first; then compare, and mark what you missed.

What the answer notes are, and are not

They are not model essays to memorise. They are the points that earn the marks: the definition, the reason, the example, the labelled part, the formula, the substitution, the unit.

If your answer contains those points in a sensible order and in your own words, it scores full marks.

3.1 Scientific Learning

1. Write any two differences between a hypothesis and a conclusion. [2]

A hypothesis is a testable guess made before the experiment; a conclusion is a judgement made after analysing the data. A hypothesis may turn out false; a conclusion is supported by the evidence collected.

2. Why is a control used in an experiment? [2]

The control is the set-up in which the factor being tested is absent or unchanged. Comparing the test with the control shows that any difference is caused by that factor and not by something else.

3. A student measured the mass of a stone as 150 g and found that it raised the water in a measuring cylinder from 50 ml to 110 ml. Find its density. [2]

Volume = 110 - 50 = 60 cm³; density = \frac{150}{60} = 2.5 g/cm³.

4. Describe the steps of the scientific method with an example. [4]

(i) Observation — the plants near the window grow taller. (ii) Problem — does light affect plant growth? (iii) Hypothesis — plants grow taller with more light.

(iv) Experiment — two identical pots, one in light and one in the dark, same soil and water. (v) Analysis — measure and compare the heights after two weeks. (vi) Conclusion — accept or reject the hypothesis on the evidence.

Note that only light is changed; soil, water and seed are controlled.

3.2 Information and Communication Technology

1. Differentiate between a scanner and a printer with one example of each. [2]

A scanner is an input device that converts a printed paper document or picture (hard copy) into a digital file (soft copy) inside a computer (e.g. flatbed scanner).

A printer is an output device that converts a digital file (soft copy) from a computer into printed text or pictures on paper (hard copy) (e.g. laser or ink-jet printer).

2. Differentiate between a search engine and a web browser with two examples of each. [2]

A search engine is a web-based software system that searches the internet for keywords and returns a list of matching web pages (e.g. Google, Bing).

A web browser is an application program installed on a device used to open and display websites and web pages (e.g. Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox).

3. Mention any four precautions to follow for safe and ethical use of social media and the internet (computer code of conduct). [4]

(i) Use a strong, mixed password (letters, digits, symbols), enable two-factor authentication, and never share your PIN or OTP with anyone.

(ii) Do not post personal details or share another person's photograph/video without their consent. (iii) Never click suspicious links or attachments (phishing/malware) and always log out of public computers or ATMs after use.

(iv) Respect cyber law (Nepal's Electronic Transactions Act 2063 BS), avoid cyberbullying or spreading fake news, and report online harassment immediately.

4. What are Artificial Intelligence (AI), Virtual Reality (VR), Robotics and Cloud Computing? Write one practical use of each. [4]

  • Artificial Intelligence (AI): computer systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence such as speech recognition, medical diagnosis and voice assistants (Siri, chatbots).
  • Virtual Reality (VR): a computer-generated 3D simulated environment experienced through a VR headset, used for flight/surgical training and virtual tours.
  • Robotics: the branch of technology that designs programmable automatic machines (robots, such as humanoid robot Sophia) used in industrial manufacturing, hazardous mining and space exploration.
  • Cloud Computing: storing and processing data on remote internet servers (such as Google Drive or iCloud) so files can be backed up and accessed from anywhere.

3.3 Living Beings and Their Structure

1. Write any two differences between a plant cell and an animal cell. [2]

A plant cell has a rigid cellulose cell wall; an animal cell has only the cell membrane. A plant cell has chloroplasts and one large vacuole; an animal cell has no chloroplasts and small vacuoles if any.

2. Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell? [2]

Cellular respiration takes place in it: food is oxidised there and the energy released is stored in a usable form for all the cell's activities. A cell with more energy demand, such as a muscle cell, has more mitochondria.

3. Write the functions of any four cell organelles. [4]

Nucleus — controls all activities and carries the hereditary material. Mitochondrion — releases energy by respiration. Ribosome — makes protein. Chloroplast — carries out photosynthesis in plant cells.

(Vacuole — stores water, food and waste and keeps the plant cell turgid.)

4. What is classification? Write the five kingdoms with one example of each. [4]

Classification is the arrangement of living beings into groups according to their similarities and differences, so that they can be studied, named and compared systematically.

Whittaker's five kingdoms (1969): Monera — bacteria; Protista — Amoeba; Fungi — mushroom; Plantae — fern; Animalia — frog.

3.4 Biodiversity and Environment

1. Define ecosystem and name its two components. [2]

An ecosystem is a unit in which living beings interact with one another and with their non-living surroundings. Its components are biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic (sunlight, air, water, soil, temperature).

2. Why is Nepal said to be rich in biodiversity in spite of its small area? [2]

Within about 200 km from south to north the land rises from about 60 m to 8,849 m, so tropical, subtropical, temperate, subalpine and alpine climates all occur. Each belt supports its own plants and animals, so a small country holds many kinds of habitat.

3. Draw a food chain of four links from a Nepali farmland and explain the flow of energy. [4]

Chain: paddy → grasshopper → frog → snake. The paddy plant is the producer, trapping sunlight. The grasshopper is the primary consumer, the frog the secondary consumer, the snake the tertiary consumer.

Energy flows in one direction only, and roughly 10 % passes from one level to the next; the rest is lost mainly as heat. That is why a chain rarely has more than four or five links.

4. Write any four causes of loss of biodiversity and one measure against each. [4]

(i) Habitat destruction by clearing forest for settlement — declare and manage protected areas, plan settlement. (ii) Poaching and illegal trade — enforce the law, support anti-poaching patrols, raise awareness.

(iii) Pollution of rivers and soil — treat waste, reduce chemical fertiliser and pesticide. (iv) Invasive species such as lahare banmara — remove them early and plant native species.

(Climate change — reduce emissions and conserve forests.)

3.5 Life Process

1. Write the word equation of photosynthesis and name two conditions needed for it. [2]

Carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight, give glucose + oxygen. Conditions: sunlight and chlorophyll (carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials).

2. Write any two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration. [2]

Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen and releases much more energy, giving carbon dioxide and water. Anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen and releases less energy, giving ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast or lactic acid in muscle.

3. Explain the path of food through the human alimentary canal. [4]

Mouth — teeth break food; saliva begins starch digestion. Oesophagus — pushes the bolus down by peristalsis. Stomach — gastric juice with hydrochloric acid and pepsin begins protein digestion.

Small intestine — bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic and intestinal juices complete digestion, and the villi absorb the nutrients. Large intestine — absorbs water and salts; the remaining waste is passed out as faeces.

4. What is transpiration? Write its importance to the plant and any two factors that affect its rate. [4]

Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata. Importance: it pulls water and dissolved minerals up from the root (transpiration pull) and cools the leaf.

Factors: temperature and humidity (also wind speed, light and the number of open stomata) — the rate rises in hot, dry, windy weather and falls in humid, still air.

3.6 Force and Motion

1. State Newton's second law of motion and write its mathematical form. [2]

The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net force applied and takes place in the direction of that force. For constant mass, F = ma, where F is the net force in newtons, m the mass in kilograms and a the acceleration in m/s².

2. Write any two differences between mass and weight. [2]

Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, measured in kilograms, and is the same everywhere. Weight is the force with which the earth attracts the body, measured in newtons, and changes with the value of g — on the moon it is about one-sixth of the value on the earth.

3. A bus starting from rest reaches 20 m/s in 10 s. Find its acceleration and the force on it if its mass is 3,000 kg. [4]

a = \frac{v-u}{t} = \frac{20-0}{10} = 2 m/s². F = ma = 3000\times2 = 6000 N, in the direction of motion.

4. Why do passengers lurch forward when a moving bus brakes suddenly? Explain with the law involved and write two safety measures based on it. [4]

By Newton's first law, a body continues in its state of motion unless a net force acts on it.

When the brakes act, the force stops the bus but not the upper part of the passenger's body, which continues forward — this is inertia of motion.

Measures: wear the seat belt so the force reaches the body with the vehicle; fit head rests and avoid standing in a fast-moving vehicle; and keep a safe following distance so braking can be gradual.

3.7 Energy in Daily Life

1. Explain how a thermos (vacuum) flask keeps hot liquids hot and cold liquids cold for a long time. [2]

A thermos flask has a double-walled glass vessel with a vacuum between the walls (which stops heat transfer by conduction and convection), silvered mirror surfaces on the walls (which reflect heat and minimise radiation), and an insulating cork/plastic stopper and support.

2. Differentiate between a concave mirror and a convex mirror (any two points) and state why a convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles. [2]

A concave mirror has an inward-curved reflecting surface and converges parallel rays to a real focus (forming real or magnified virtual images).

A convex mirror has an outward-bulging reflecting surface and diverges parallel rays from a virtual focus.

A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror because it always forms an erect, diminished virtual image and provides a much wider field of view of traffic behind.

3. Differentiate among infrasonic, audible and ultrasonic sounds with examples. A sound wave has frequency 500\text{ Hz} and wavelength 0.68\text{ m}; find its speed. [4]

  • Infrasonic sound (infrasound): frequency below 20\text{ Hz} (cannot be heard by humans; produced by earthquakes, elephants, whales).
  • Audible sound: frequency between 20\text{ Hz} and 20\text{ kHz} (20,000\text{ Hz}), which the human ear can detect.
  • Ultrasonic sound (ultrasound): frequency above 20\text{ kHz} (produced by bats, dolphins, SONAR and medical ultrasound scanners).
  • Calculation: Speed of sound v = f \times \lambda = 500 \times 0.68 = \mathbf{340\text{ m/s}}.

4. What is the greenhouse effect? Write any two causes and two control measures of sound (noise) pollution. [4]

The greenhouse effect is the trapping of solar infrared heat radiation by greenhouse gases (\text{CO}_2, \text{CH}_4, \text{N}_2\text{O}, water vapour) in the earth's atmosphere or inside a glass/plastic greenhouse, keeping the interior warm.

Causes of noise pollution: loud vehicle horns and engines, industrial machinery, loudspeakers and construction work.

Control measures: plant green belt trees along roads, ban pressure horns near schools/hospitals, use silencers and sound-absorbing materials in factories.

3.8 Electricity and Magnetism

1. State two main postulates of the molecular theory of magnetism. Why does heating or hammering a magnet demagnetise it? [2]

(i) Every magnetic substance consists of tiny molecular magnets, each having N and S poles. (ii) In an unmagnetised bar they form random closed chains, whereas in a magnetised bar they align in parallel open chains.

Heating or hammering increases molecular vibration and breaks the parallel alignment back into closed chains, causing demagnetisation.

2. What is terrestrial magnetism? Why is the earth pin in a three-pin plug made longer and thicker than the other two pins? [2]

Terrestrial magnetism is the natural magnetic field of the earth, which behaves like a huge bar magnet whose magnetic south pole lies near the geographical north.

The earth pin in a 3-pin plug is longer so that it makes contact first (earthing the appliance before live current enters) and disconnects last, and thicker so it has low resistance for fault current and cannot be accidentally inserted into the live hole.

3. A house uses four 60\text{ W} bulbs for 5\text{ hours} and a 1,000\text{ W} heater for 2\text{ hours} each day. Find the daily consumption in units and the monthly bill at Rs 10 per unit for 30\text{ days}. [4]

Bulbs: 4\times60 = 240\text{ W} = 0.24\text{ kW}, for 5\text{ h} = 1.2\text{ kWh}. Heater: 1\text{ kW} for 2\text{ h} = 2\text{ kWh}. Daily total = 3.2\text{ units}. Monthly = 3.2\times30 = 96\text{ units}; bill = 96\times10 = Rs 960.

4. Differentiate between a fuse and an MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker). Explain the roles of the live (phase), neutral and earth wires in domestic wiring. [4]

A fuse is a thin low-melting-point wire (tin-lead alloy) that melts and must be replaced after an overload/short circuit; an MCB is an automatic electromagnetic switch that trips off on overload and can simply be switched back ON.

Live (phase) wire (red/brown): carries current at 220\text{ V} from the mains to the appliance (switches and fuses are placed here). Neutral wire (black/blue): completes the return path at 0\text{ V}.

Earth wire (green/yellow): connects the metal casing of an appliance to the ground to prevent electric shock from leakage current.

3.9 Matter

1. An element has atomic number 19 and mass number 39. Find its protons, electrons, neutrons, shell electronic configuration (2n^2 rule) and valency. [2]

Protons = 19, electrons = 19, neutrons = 39 - 19 = 20. Shell electronic configuration (K, L, M, N): 2, 8, 8, 1 (Potassium, \text{K}). Since it has 1 valence electron in its outermost shell, its valency is 1.

2. Write the molecular formulae of (i) magnesium chloride and (ii) aluminium oxide by the criss-cross method, and find the molecular weight of \text{CaCO}_3 (\text{Ca}=40, \text{C}=12, \text{O}=16). [2]

(i) \text{Mg} (valency 2) and \text{Cl} (valency 1) \rightarrow \mathbf{\text{MgCl}_2}. (ii) \text{Al} (valency 3) and \text{O} (valency 2) \rightarrow \mathbf{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}.

Molecular weight of \text{CaCO}_3 = 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 40 + 12 + 48 = \mathbf{100\text{ amu}}.

3. State the Modern Periodic Law. How do (i) number of shells, (ii) atomic size, (iii) valency and (iv) metallic character vary across a period and down a group? [4]

Modern Periodic Law (Moseley): The physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. (i) Number of shells: remains the same across a period, increases by one down a group.

(ii) Atomic size: decreases left to right across a period (greater nuclear pull), increases down a group (new shell added). (iii) Valency: remains the same in a group; across a period increases from 1 to 4 then decreases from 3 to 0.

(iv) Metallic character: decreases across a period, increases down a group.

4. Convert the following word equations into balanced chemical equations: [4] (a) Hydrogen + Oxygen \rightarrow Water (b) Zinc + Dilute hydrochloric acid \rightarrow Zinc chloride + Hydrogen

(a) \mathbf{2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}} (b) \mathbf{\text{Zn} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{ZnCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\uparrow}

3.10 Materials Used in Daily Life

1. Differentiate between temporary hardness and permanent hardness of water, and write one method to remove each. [2]

Temporary hardness is caused by dissolved bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium (\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2, \text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2) and can be removed by boiling or Clark's method (adding slaked lime).

Permanent hardness is caused by dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (\text{CaCl}_2, \text{CaSO}_4, \text{MgCl}_2, \text{MgSO}_4) and is removed by adding washing soda (\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) or by the permutit (zeolite) process.

2. What is an alloy? Write the constituent elements and one daily-life use of brass, bronze and stainless steel. [2]

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with one or more other metals or non-metals made to improve hardness, strength and corrosion resistance. Brass (\text{Cu} + \text{Zn}): utensils, taps, locks.

Bronze (\text{Cu} + \text{Sn}): statues, medals, temple bells. Stainless steel (\text{Fe} + \text{Cr} + \text{Ni} + \text{C}): surgical instruments and kitchen cutlery.

3. What are acids, bases and salts? Give the colour changes of litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein in acidic and basic solutions. [4]

Acids yield \text{H}^+ ions in water and taste sour; bases yield \text{OH}^- ions (in alkalis) and taste bitter/soapy; salts are formed by neutralisation of an acid with a base (\text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}). - Litmus: red in acid, blue in base. - Methyl orange: red (pinkish) in acid, yellow in base. - Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base.

4. What is acid rain? Write its causes, two harmful effects on the environment, and two control measures. [4]

Acid rain is rainwater with \text{pH} < 5.6 formed when air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide (\text{SO}_2) and nitrogen oxides (\text{NO}_2) from factories and vehicles react with rainwater to form sulphuric acid (\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) and nitric acid (\text{HNO}_3).

Harmful effects: corrodes marble/limestone monuments (marble cancer) and metal roofs; makes soil and lakes acidic, killing fish and crops.

Control: use clean renewable energy, fit scrubbers/catalytic converters in factories and vehicles.

3.11 The Earth and Universe

1. Define a mineral. Name two metallic and two non-metallic minerals found in Nepal along with their locations. [2]

A mineral is a naturally occurring homogeneous solid substance in the earth's crust with a definite chemical composition.

Metallic minerals in Nepal: Iron ore (Phulchoki in Lalitpur, Thoshe in Ramechhap), Copper ore (Udayapur, Makwanpur), Lead/Zinc (Ganesh Himal). Non-metallic minerals: Limestone (Udayapur, Chobhar), Magnesite (Dolakha), Coal (Dang).

2. Differentiate among meteoroids, meteors (shooting stars) and meteorites, and name the three parts of a comet. [2]

Meteoroids are small rocky or metallic fragments travelling in space; when one enters the earth's atmosphere and burns with a bright streak of light due to air friction it is called a meteor (shooting star); if an unburnt fragment reaches the earth's surface it is called a meteorite.

A comet consists of a solid icy nucleus, a glowing gaseous coma, and a long tail pointing away from the sun.

3. State the Big Bang theory of the origin of the universe and name any two hypotheses of the origin of the earth. [4]

According to the Big Bang theory (Georges Lemaître), about 13.8\text{ billion years} ago all matter and energy of the universe were concentrated in a tiny, super-dense, super-hot primeval atom (singularity) which exploded violently; as the universe expanded and cooled, galaxies, stars and planetary systems formed, and galaxies are still moving apart today.

Hypotheses of the origin of the earth: (i) Kant–Laplace Nebular Hypothesis (rotating hot gaseous nebula cooled and shed rings that condensed into planets) and (ii) Jeans–Jeffreys Tidal Hypothesis (a passing star pulled a cigar-shaped filament of gas from the sun).

4. Name the four major geological eras in chronological order and mention the dominant life forms that evolved in each era. [4]

  1. Precambrian Era (origin of earth \sim 4.5\text{ billion} to 570\text{ million} years ago): origin of first unicellular prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae) and soft-bodied marine invertebrates in the oceans.
  2. Palaeozoic Era (570\text{–}250\text{ million} years ago): age of marine invertebrates, fishes, amphibians, and giant spore-bearing ferns (pteridophytes).
  3. Mesozoic Era (250\text{–}65\text{ million} years ago): "Age of Reptiles" — origin, dominance and extinction of dinosaurs, predominance of gymnosperms (conifers), and first birds (Archaeopteryx) and early mammals.
  4. Cenozoic Era (65\text{ million} years ago to present): "Age of Mammals and Angiosperms" — rapid evolution of modern mammals, birds, flowering plants, and human beings (Homo sapiens).
Writing for marks

Read every answer above and count its points. Two marks, two points; four marks, four points. If your own answer has fewer, the content is missing, not the handwriting. If it has more, you are spending time you will need for Group C.

3.12 Extended model answers (8 to 10 marks)

The Science paper rewards a complete answer: an introduction, a labelled diagram or table, points in order, and a one-line conclusion. The three model answers below show the full length expected when a question carries 8 to 10 marks.

Extended questions

  1. What is a cell? Describe the structure of a plant cell and an animal cell and differentiate between them. [10]
  2. Define photosynthesis and respiration. Write the equation of each and differentiate between the two processes. [10]
  3. Differentiate between a series and a parallel circuit. Two resistors of 4 Ω and 8 Ω are joined to a 12 V battery; find the current in each arrangement. [10]

Model answer D1: plant cell and animal cell (10 marks)

Introduction. A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of a living thing.

Robert Hooke first saw cells in a thin slice of cork in 1665, and later work showed that all plants, animals and microbes are made of one or more cells.

A bacterium or Paramecium is a single cell, while a human body has trillions of them. Cells are seen only through a microscope, as in the figure above.

Structure of a typical cell. Both plant and animal cells contain the following parts.

  1. Cell membrane. A thin, flexible skin that surrounds the cell and decides which substances may enter or leave. It is the outer boundary in an animal cell.
  2. Cytoplasm. A jelly-like fluid in which the other parts float. Most chemical reactions of the cell take place here.
  3. Nucleus. The control centre of the cell. It holds the chromosomes that carry the instructions for growth and inheritance.
  4. Mitochondria. Tiny structures that release energy from food during respiration. They are called the powerhouse of the cell.
  5. Vacuole. A fluid-filled space that stores water, food and waste. It is small and many in an animal cell, but large and single in a mature plant cell.

Extra parts found only in a plant cell. A cell wall of cellulose lies outside the membrane and gives a fixed shape and strength. Chloroplasts hold the green pigment chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis.

These two parts are why a leaf is green and a tree stands upright.

Difference between a plant cell and an animal cell

Feature Plant cell Animal cell
Cell wall Present (cellulose) Absent
Shape Fixed, usually regular Irregular, can change
Chloroplast Present in green parts Absent
Vacuole One large central vacuole Small and many, or none
Food Makes its own food Takes ready-made food
Centrioles Usually absent Present
Example Onion root, leaf cell Cheek cell, blood cell

Conclusion. The cell wall and chloroplasts separate a plant cell from an animal cell, while the membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria are common to both. Knowing these parts explains why plants are producers and animals are consumers.

Model answer D2: photosynthesis and respiration (10 marks)

Introduction. Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight absorbed by chlorophyll.

Respiration is the process by which living cells break down glucose to release energy for work. The two processes are opposite in direction, and together they keep the oxygen and carbon dioxide of the air in balance.

Photosynthesis.

  1. Raw materials are carbon dioxide from the air, taken in through the stomata, and water, taken from the soil by the roots.
  2. Sunlight is the source of energy, and chlorophyll in the chloroplasts traps it.
  3. The products are glucose, which is stored as starch, and oxygen, which is given out to the air.
  4. It takes place only in the green parts of the plant and only in light.

Equation: carbon dioxide + water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen, that is, 6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2.

Respiration.

  1. The raw materials are glucose and oxygen.
  2. The energy is released slowly, step by step, in the mitochondria and stored as ATP.
  3. The products are carbon dioxide, water and energy. Some energy escapes as heat, which keeps our body warm.
  4. It happens in every living cell, day and night.

Equation: C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{energy}.

Difference between photosynthesis and respiration

Basis Photosynthesis Respiration
Where Only green cells with chloroplasts All living cells
Time Only in the light Day and night
Raw materials Carbon dioxide and water Glucose and oxygen
Energy Light energy is stored in glucose Energy is released from glucose
Gas exchange Takes in CO₂, gives out O₂ Takes in O₂, gives out CO₂
Type of reaction Builds food (constructive) Breaks food down (destructive)
Effect on mass Dry mass of the plant increases Dry mass decreases

Conclusion. Photosynthesis stores the sun's energy in food and fills the air with oxygen, and respiration releases that energy for life. This is why forests such as Chitwan are called the lungs of the earth, and why planting trees keeps the air of Kathmandu cleaner.

Model answer D3: series and parallel circuits (10 marks)

Introduction. An electric circuit is a closed path along which charge flows. When more than one resistor or bulb is used, they can be joined end to end (series) or side by side between the same two points (parallel).

Household wiring in Nepal is parallel, while old festival lights were often wired in series.

Series circuit.

  1. The components are joined one after another, so there is only one path for the current.
  2. The same current flows through every component.
  3. The battery voltage is shared: V = V_1 + V_2.
  4. The total resistance is the sum: R = R_1 + R_2.
  5. If one bulb fuses, the whole circuit breaks and all bulbs go off.

Parallel circuit.

  1. Each component is joined across the same two points, so there are several paths.
  2. The voltage across every branch equals the battery voltage.
  3. The current divides: I = I_1 + I_2.
  4. The total resistance is less than the smallest resistor: \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}.
  5. If one bulb fuses, the others keep glowing.

Difference table

Basis Series Parallel
Paths for current One More than one
Current Same in all Divides among branches
Voltage Divides Same across all
Total resistance Large (sum) Small (less than the least)
One part fails Whole circuit stops Other parts still work
Use Fuse with a switch, torch cells House wiring

Numerical. A 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor are joined to a 12 V battery. By Ohm's law, I = V/R.

  1. Series: R = 4 + 8 = 12\ \Omega, so I = 12/12 = 1 A in both resistors. The voltages are 4\times1 = 4 V and 8\times1 = 8 V, which add to 12 V.
  2. Parallel: each resistor has 12 V. I_1 = 12/4 = 3 A, I_2 = 12/8 = 1.5 A, and the total current is 4.5 A. The equivalent resistance is \frac{4\times8}{4+8} = 2.67\ \Omega, and 12/2.67 = 4.5 A, which checks.

Conclusion. In series the current is shared by all and the voltage is divided, while in parallel the voltage is shared and the current is divided. That is why every house is wired in parallel: each appliance gets the full 220 V and works on its own.
